analysis.one_liner: Bans nursing homes from forcing residents to sign away their right to sue before disputes arise.
analysis.headline: Introduced with a Republican sponsor and Democratic cosponsors in March 2009, the bill never got a hearing or vote and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing homes commonly require residents or their families to sign an arbitration agreement at admission, before any dispute exists. That agreement sends future claims — including cases of neglect, abuse, or wrongful death — to a private arbitrator chosen under the facility's contract instead of a court, where proceedings are private, appeals are limited, and damages can be smaller. This bill would amend federal arbitration law to make such pre-dispute agreements between long-term care facilities and residents unenforceable, leaving residents free to sue in court and to decide on arbitration only after a dispute arises.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families, who keep the option of a public court case with a jury, open records, and full appeals if a facility injures or neglects them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes any pre-dispute arbitration agreement between a long-term care facility and a resident (or anyone acting for the resident, including a person with financial responsibility) invalid and unenforceable [S2][S3].

It covers agreements signed during admission or at any later time, and applies to skilled nursing facilities, nursing facilities, and assisted-living-type facilities that provide help with daily activities such as bathing, dressing, eating, and taking medication [S3].
It puts the decision about whether the federal rule applies in the hands of a court rather than an arbitrator, closing a common route by which facilities force challenges into arbitration [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Long-term care facilities, which would lose a tool for keeping injury and death cases out of court and could face more jury trials and larger verdicts; the arbitration industry loses a steady stream of mandated business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and arbitration firms

drawbacks.text: Defenders of arbitration clauses argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for small claims, and that some facilities might raise prices or adjust contracts to cover added litigation risk [S1].
The ban is categorical: it applies to every long-term care facility and every resident, including cases where a resident or family might have preferred arbitration on its merits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the population covered — elderly and disabled people in facilities who sign admission paperwork under pressure and often cannot read the fine print — the trade is heavily one-sided: the cost falls on facility litigation budgets, and the benefit is access to the courts for the most serious cases of neglect and abuse. The main honest objection is that the bill is broad rather than tailored, but it does not ban arbitration after a dispute arises; it only bars facilities from demanding arbitration before anything has gone wrong.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on its first day, and nothing further ever happened — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Mel Martinez (R-FL) introduced the bill on March 3, 2009, with Herb Kohl, Dick Durbin, and Russ Feingold listed as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
Six Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill, alongside its Republican sponsor [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
The action history shows no further steps: no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote, through the end of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators are better off: they kept the ability to have residents sign arbitration agreements at admission, keeping injury and death cases out of court. Families of residents gained nothing; the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators who kept forced arbitration

industries.industry: Nursing home and long-term care industry
industries.note: The bill would bar facilities from having residents sign arbitration agreements at admission, which would expose neglect and abuse cases to public courts, juries, and appeals instead of private arbitration. The industry's interest in keeping those cases private runs against residents' interest in accountability.
The bill removes a mandated stream of arbitration business from nursing home contracts. Arbitrators' fees come out of residents' purses in disputes that would otherwise be heard in court at no fee.
